These negative impacts will be balanced to a greater or lesser degree through positive returns resulting from use of the land affected for recreational purposes, for production of game species compatible with the endangered species, and for research and educational purposes.
Economic impact will occur from mining and petroleum extraction that is postponed or not carried out because it might prevent the restoration of an endangered species. Such extractions of minerals and petroleum include in their adverse effects the direct destruction of endangered species habitat, the pollution of nearby waters, and harmful disturbance to endangered animals from human activity surrounding the mining site.
Limited losses of livestock and crops may have to be accepted as a part of the cost of restoration of some endangered species such as the larger predators. Because the endangered predators will be few in actual numbers, the total losses will be relatively small. But losses on a local basis and to individuals could be significant. One of the threats facing the endangered red wolf in southeastern Texas is the killing of wolves by farmers and ranchers who retaliate for depredations on their domestic livestock. One objective of the red wolf restoration program is to persuade the owners and society to accept these losses as part of the cost of doing business just as they absorb losses due to weather. The same would be an objective of the Utah prairie dog restoration program when farmers retaliate for crop depredations by poisoning prairie dog colonies. Some compensation may be achieved by acquisition of lands harboring the endangered prairie dogs.
